payload.name: cricothyroid-membrane
payload.scope: People made the cricothyroid membrane construct to map the fibrous sheet between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, so that clinicians can identify the emergency airway landmark and the vocal ligament's relationship to the airway wall.

definition.body: The cricothyroid membrane is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the fibrous sheet between the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage and the complete superior border of the cricoid cartilage, forming the floor of the laryngeal cavity and the landmark of the emergency surgical airway. Parameters: (1) the boundaries - superiorly the inferior border of the thyroid laminae, inferiorly the superior border of the cricoid lamina, laterally blending into the cricothyroid joint capsules; (2) the composition - a fibroelastic sheet, thin and transparent anteriorly, with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal vessels passing on its deep surface; (3) the relationships - its free superior border thickens into the vocal ligament, and the submucosa above it carries the laryngeal mucosa; (4) the clinical access - the site of needle cricothyroidotomy and percutaneous dilational cricothyroidotomy, the standard emergency airway when intubation fails. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, emergency airway protocols, and laryngeal surgical planning documents. e.g.: cricothyroid membrane puncture for needle cricothyroidotomy per ATLS 10th edition; the membrane shown in the larynx chapter of Moore Clinically Orientated Anatomy 9th edition; the membrane as the entry point of percutaneous cricothyroidotomy in the ASA difficult airway algorithm | not: the cricoid cartilage (the complete ring forming its inferior border, a distinct structure); the thyrohyoid membrane (the membrane above it between thyroid and hyoid); the cricothyroid joint (the articulation between the cartilages, lateral to the membrane) [formal: membrana cricothyroidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Parameters: (1) the boundaries - above the laryngeal inlet (epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoid cartilages), below the free edges of the true vocal folds, laterally opening to the piriform recesses which continue into the pharynx and lie outside this boundary; (2) the contents - the pre-epiglottic space anterior to the epiglottis and the laryngeal ventricle between the vestibular and vocal folds lie within it; (3) the clinical significance - the supraglottic compartment that closes during swallowing as the vestibular folds approximate over it, and the region of supraglottic obstruction treated by supraglottic stenting. payload.name: pharynx
payload.scope: People made the pharynx construct to map the muscular tube connecting the nasal and oral cavities to the larynx and esophagus, so that clinicians can localize lesions, plan surgical approaches, and manage airway obstruction at the crossroads of the respiratory and digestive tracts.

definition.body: The pharynx is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the muscular tube that connects the posterior nasal apertures and oral cavity to the larynx and esophagus, serving both the respiratory and digestive pathways. Parameters: (1) the superior-to-inferior divisions — nasopharynx (behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate), oropharynx (behind the oral cavity, between the soft palate and epiglottis), and laryngopharynx/hypopharynx (behind the larynx, from the epiglottis to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage where it continues as the esophagus); (2) the muscular walls — three constrictor muscles (superior, middle, inferior) arranged in overlapping tiers plus longitudinal muscles (stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus) that elevate the pharynx and larynx during swallowing; (3) the compartments — the aerodigestive conduit that separates respiratory from digestive flow via the soft palate, epiglottis, and pharyngeal constrictor coordination; (4) the clinical landmarks — Waldeyer ring of lymphoid tissue (adenoids, palatine tonsils, lingual tonsil), the pharyngeal recess of Fossa of Rosenmüller, the esophageal opening. It persists as a maintained anatomical region in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology, and head-and-neck surgical atlases. e.g.: the pharynx as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; nasopharyngeal carcinoma staging per the AJCC 8th edition using the pharyngeal recess; pharyngeal manometry measuring superior, middle, and inferior constrictor pressures | not: the esophagus (the digestive tube continuing from the pharynx at the cricoid level, distinct pathway); the trachea (the respiratory tube continuing from the larynx at the carina, distinct pathway); the oral cavity (the space anterior to the oropharynx, separated by the fauces) [formal: pharynx | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: hypopharynx
payload.scope: People made the hypopharynx construct to map the inferior portion of the pharynx behind the larynx, so that clinicians can localize and stage cancers, assess swallowing dysfunction, and plan surgical reconstruction of the aerodigestive junction.

definition.body: The hypopharynx (also called the laryngopharynx) is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the inferior division of the pharynx that lies posterior to the larynx, extending from the epiglottis superiorly to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage inferiorly where it continues as the esophagus. Parameters: (1) the four subsites — postcricoid region (posterior to the cricoid cartilage, anterior to the esophagus), bilateral pyriform sinuses (lateral recesses lateral to the laryngeal inlet, bounded medially by the aryepiglottic fold and laterally by the thyroid cartilage), the posterior pharyngeal wall behind the larynx, and the laryngeal inlet (the opening from the oropharynx into the laryngopharynx bounded by the epiglottis and arytenoids); (2) the mucosal lining — stratified squamous epithelium continuous with both esophageal and laryngeal mucosa; (3) the muscular layer — continuous with the pharyngeal constrictors longitudinally and the superior esophageal sphincter inferiorly; (4) the neurovascular supply — internal laryngeal nerve (sensory, from superior laryngeal branch of vagus), recurrent laryngeal nerve, and superior laryngeal vessels; (5) the clinical significance — common site of squamous cell carcinoma, region assessed during swallowing evaluation, landmark for esophageal opening. It persists as a maintained anatomical region in head-and-neck anatomy, oncology staging systems, and otolaryngology. e.g.: the hypopharynx subsites mapped in TNM staging (AJCC 8th edition) for hypopharyngeal carcinoma; a barium swallow study demonstrating a pyriform sinus filling defect; postcricoid web identified on upper endoscopy | not: the pyriform-fossa (the lateral recess specifically, a subsite of the hypopharynx); the esophagus (the tube continuing from the hypopharynx at the cricoid level, distinct pathway); the larynx (the organ anterior to the hypopharynx containing the vocal folds, distinct functional system) [formal: hypopharynx | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vallecula

definition.body: The vallecula (epiglottic vallecula) is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired shallow depressions between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis, bounded medially by the median glossoepiglottic fold and laterally opening into the piriform sinuses. Parameters: (1) the anatomical boundaries — anteriorly the posterior surface of the epiglottis, posteriorly the base of the tongue (posterior third, above the circumvallate papillae), bounded medially by the median glossoepiglottic fold and laterally by the lateral glossoepiglottic folds; (2) the bilateral nature — a left and right vallecular space separated by the median fold; (3) the clinical significance — blind spot on routine laryngoscopy that requires epiglottic elevation to visualize, common site for vallecular cysts that can cause airway obstruction, landmark for determining laryngoscopic view (Mallampati classification uses vallecular space to grade airway difficulty), injection site for topical local anesthesia in awake intubation; (4) the developmental anatomy — vallecular cysts arise from obstruction of minor salivary glands in the vallecular mucosa. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in airway management guidelines, otolaryngology texts, and anesthesia reference atlases. e.g.: the valleculae visualized during direct laryngoscopy using a Macintosh blade in Miller's Anesthesia 9th edition; a vallecular cyst causing obstructive sleep apnea imaged on MRI per the Laryngoscope; Mallampati class determination by visualizing the vallecular space in the ASA difficult airway algorithm | not: the piriform-fossa (the lateral recess lateral to the laryngeal inlet, separated by the aryepiglottic fold); the circumvallate-papillae (the row of taste buds anterior to the vallecula on the tongue base, distinct structure) [formal: vallecula | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: thyrohyoid-membrane
payload.scope: People made the thyrohyoid membrane construct to map the fibrous sheet connecting the hyoid bone to the thyroid cartilage, so that clinicians can identify the superior boundary of the anterior laryngeal wall and navigate surgical approaches in the suprahyoid neck.

definition.body: The thyrohyoid membrane is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the broad fibrous sheet extending between the superior border of the thyroid cartilage and the hyoid bone. Parameters: (1) the attachments — inferiorly attached to the superior border and superior horns of the thyroid cartilage, superiorly to the superior margin and tips of the greater horns of the hyoid bone; (2) the composition — a broad fibrous sheet with a thicker anterior margin and thinner posterior portions; (3) the relationships — anteriorly continuous with the infrahyoid musculature, posteriorly opens into a slit-like interval (the thyrohyoid hiatus) through which the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels pass; (4) the lateral thickening — the lateral margins thicken into the thyrohyoid ligament, which provides the primary structural connection between the hyoid and thyroid cartilages; (5) the clinical access — a landmark for the thyrohyoid membrane puncture technique in percutaneous tracheostomy and a surgical approach window in anterior neck dissection. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, head and neck surgical atlases, and airway management guidelines. e.g.: the thyrohyoid membrane described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the thyrohyoid membrane as a surgical landmark in anterior neck dissection per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; percutaneous tracheostomy via thyrohyoid membrane puncture in the journal of Critical Care Medicine [formal: membrana thyrohyoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: People made the conus elasticus construct to map the conical fibrous membrane connecting the cricoid cartilage to the thyroid cartilage and vocal ligaments, so that clinicians can understand the structural continuity of the laryngeal framework and the pathway for the internal laryngeal nerve.

definition.body: The conus elasticus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the conical sheet of elastic connective tissue extending between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, forming the walls of the subglottic region. Parameters: (1) the origin — arises from the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage, attaching to its entire superior margin; (2) the attachments — ascends anteriorly to the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage, laterally to the vocal ligaments and vocal processes of the arytenoid cartilages, and posteriorly to the interarytenoid muscles; (3) the composition — predominantly elastic fibers with some collagen, thicker inferiorly and tapering as it ascends; (4) the relationships — continuous superiorly with the cricothyroid membrane and with the vocal ligaments (which form its free upper borders), continuous inferiorly with the subglottic mucosa; (5) the clinical relevance — defines the boundaries of the subglottis, a common site for subglottic stenosis, and serves as a surgical landmark during laryngeal procedures. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and head and neck surgical planning documents. e.g.: the conus elasticus described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake, Hauser and Carucci; the conus elasticus as the structural basis of the vocal ligament in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; surgical resection of conus elasticus in laryngeal trauma reconstruction per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition [formal: conus elasticus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: hyoid-bone
payload.scope: People made the hyoid bone construct to map the U-shaped bone in the anterior neck that serves as the primary attachment point for muscles of the tongue, pharynx, and larynx, so that clinicians can identify the key bony landmark for airway manipulation and surgical access in the neck.

definition.body: The hyoid bone is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the U-shaped bone in the anterior neck at the level of C3, serving as a floating anchor between the mandible and the larynx. Parameters: (1) the architecture — composed of a body, greater horns (cornua), and lesser horns (cornua), with the greater horns extending posterolaterally from the body; (2) the suspensory attachments — suspended from the styloid processes of the temporal bones by the stylohyoid ligaments and from the mandible by the mylohyoid muscle; (3) the muscular attachments — anteriorly by the suprahyoid muscles (mylohyoid, geniohyoid, digastric, stylohyoid), inferiorly by the infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid); (4) the relationships — lies superior to the thyroid cartilage and laryngeal inlet, anterior to the pharyngeal wall, and connected to the epiglottis by the thyrohyoid membrane; (5) the clinical relevance — a critical landmark in anterior neck surgery, used as a reference for thyroid and parathyroid surgery, and a common site of fracture in strangulation and manual choking. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, head and neck surgical atlases, and forensic medicine references. e.g.: the hyoid bone described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake, Hauser and Carucci; the hyoid bone as a surgical landmark in thyroidectomy per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; forensic analysis of hyoid bone fracture in strangulation cases per the American Journal of Forensic Medicine [formal: os hyoideum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: corniculate-cartilage
payload.scope: Anatomical construct identifying the paired conical cartilages sitting atop the apices of the arytenoid cartilages in the larynx, contributing to the posterior aspect of the laryngeal inlet.

definition.body: The corniculate cartilages (cartilagines corniculatae) are a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired conical cartilages that sit atop the apices of the arytenoid cartilages within the larynx, forming part of the posterior laryngeal inlet and supporting the aryepiglottic folds. Parameters: (1) the position — each cartilage rests on the apex of its corresponding arytenoid cartilage; (2) the composition — elastic cartilage, continuous with the arytenoid's cartilage; (3) the relationships — embedded within the aryepiglottic fold, adjacent to the cuneiform cartilage, and contributing to the closure of the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology references, and airway management guides. e.g.: the corniculate cartilage shown in the larynx chapter of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the corniculate tubercle identified during direct laryngoscopy per Miller's Anesthesia, 9th edition; corniculate cartilage calcification noted on lateral neck radiograph in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the cuneiform cartilage (paired wedge-shaped cartilage in the aryepiglottic fold, anterior to the corniculate); the arytenoid cartilage (larger pyramid-shaped cartilage the corniculate rests upon, a distinct structure); the epiglottis (leaf-shaped cartilage forming the anterior roof of the laryngeal inlet, a distinct structure) [formal: cartilago corniculata | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: nasopharynx
payload.scope: Anatomical construct delineating the superior division of the pharynx, lying behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate, serving as the shared passage for air before it diverges into the larynx and esophagus.

definition.body: The nasopharynx is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the superior division of the pharynx, lying posterior to the nasal cavity and superior to the soft palate, forming the airway conduit between the nasal choanae and the oropharynx. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly the posterior nasal apertures (choanae), inferiorly the superior border of the soft palate, posteriorly the mucosa overlying the body of the sphenoid and the superior constrictor muscle; (2) the lymphoid tissue — the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) on the posterior wall, and the lateral pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmüller) on each lateral wall; (3) the epithelial lining — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium continuous with the nasal cavity; (4) the clinical relevance — site of adenoid hypertrophy causing nasal obstruction, and the fossa of Rosenmüller as a common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma. It persists as a standard anatomical region in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology, and head-and-neck radiology. e.g.: the nasopharynx shown in the pharynx chapter of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; nasopharyngoscopy for adenoid evaluation per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; nasopharyngeal carcinoma staging using the pharyngeal recess on MRI per AJCC 8th edition | not: the oropharynx (the middle division of the pharynx behind the oral cavity, inferior to the soft palate); the nasal cavity (the air-filled space anterior to the nasopharynx, separated by the choanae); the pharyngeal tonsil (the lymphoid tissue within the nasopharyngeal wall, a structure contained within the space) [formal: nasopharynx | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: oropharynx
payload.scope: Anatomical construct delineating the middle division of the pharynx, lying behind the oral cavity and above the epiglottis, serving as the shared passage where air and food converge before diverging into the respiratory and digestive tracts.

definition.body: The oropharynx is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the middle division of the pharynx, lying posterior to the oral cavity and between the soft palate and the epiglottis, forming the common pathway for both respiratory and digestive streams. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly the oral cavity at the fauces (the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches), superiorly the soft palate and posterior nasal cavities, posteriorly the mucosa overlying the middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles, and inferiorly the level of the hyoid bone and epiglottis; (2) the lymphoid structures — the palatine tonsils between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches, and the lingual tonsil on the posterior third of the tongue; (3) the muscular walls — three constrictor muscles (superior, middle, inferior) and longitudinal muscles (stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus); (4) the clinical relevance — site of tonsillectomy, oropharyngeal dysphagia assessment, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma. It persists as a standard anatomical region in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology, and head-and-neck surgical atlases. e.g.: the oropharynx shown in the pharynx chapter of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; oropharyngeal airway placement visualizing the tonsillar fossae per Miller's Anesthesia, 9th edition; oropharyngeal carcinoma assessed by tonsillar pillar inspection in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th ed | not: the nasopharynx (the superior division behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate); the hypopharynx (the inferior division behind the larynx, from the epiglottis to the cricoid); the oral cavity (the space anterior to the oropharynx, separated by the fauces) [formal: oropharynx | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cricotracheal-membrane
payload.scope: People made the cricotracheal membrane construct to map the fibrous connective tissue bridging the cricoid cartilage to the first tracheal ring, so that clinicians can identify this surgical landmark during airway procedures.

definition.body: The cricotracheal membrane (cricotracheal ligament) is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the fibrous band connecting the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage to the first tracheal ring, bridging the larynx and the trachea. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — superiorly the inferior border of the cricoid lamina, inferiorly the superior border of the first tracheal ring; (2) the composition — a condensed band of fibrous connective tissue, continuous with the pretracheal fascia laterally; (3) the relationships — the intermediate tracheal ligament lies anterior to it; the inferior thyroid veins and recurrent laryngeal nerves cross its anterior surface; (4) the clinical access — a landmark during tracheostomy and laryngotracheal separation procedures. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts and airway surgery references. e.g.: the cricotracheal membrane described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the cricotracheal ligament identified during tracheostomy in the ATLS 10th edition; the cricotracheal junction shown in Cummings Otolaryngology upper airway diagram, 6th edition | not: the cricothyroid membrane (sheet between thyroid and cricoid cartilages); the intermediate tracheal ligament (anterior band between cricoid and first tracheal ring) [formal: ligamentum cricotracheale | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: thyroepiglottic-ligament
payload.scope: People made the thyroepiglottic-ligament construct to map the fibrous connection between the epiglottis and the thyroid cartilage, so that laryngeal surgeons and airway clinicians can identify this landmark during surgical procedures and intubation.

definition.body: The thyroepiglottic ligament is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the fibrous band connecting the apex and lateral borders of the epiglottis to the anterior surface of the thyroid cartilage, specifically to the angle of the thyroid lamina just below the superior laryngeal nerve. Parameters: (1) the attachments — the epiglottic apex and lateral margins connected to the thyroid angle; (2) the composition — dense fibrous connective tissue, continuous with the pre-epiglottic space fat anteriorly; (3) the functional role — maintains the position of the epiglottis relative to the thyroid cartilage and transmits forces during swallowing. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology references, and surgical atlases. e.g.: the thyroepiglottic ligament described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the thyroepiglottic ligament as a surgical landmark in thyroepiglottoplasty per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the thyroepiglottic ligament visualized during microlaryngeal surgery in Miller's Anesthesia, 9th edition | not: the hyoepiglottic ligament (distinct ligament to hyoid bone); the pre-epiglottic space (fat-filled space anterior to the epiglottis) [formal: ligamentum thyroepiglotticum | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The hyoepiglottic ligament is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the fibrous band connecting the superior border and apex of the epiglottis to the body of the hyoid bone, forming the anterior boundary of the quadrangular membrane. Parameters: (1) the attachments — the hyoid bone body superiorly connected to the epiglottic apex and superior border inferiorly; (2) the composition — dense fibrous connective tissue continuous with the epiglottis mucosa and the thyrohyoid membrane; (3) the functional role — suspends the epiglottis from the hyoid bone and transmits hyoid elevation forces during swallowing to help close the laryngeal inlet. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology references, and surgical atlases. e.g.: the hyoepiglottic ligament described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the hyoepiglottic ligament as a landmark in laryngeal suspension surgery per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the hyoepiglottic ligament visualized during hyoid suspension for dysphagia in Miller's Anesthesia, 9th edition | not: the thyroepiglottic ligament (connects the epiglottis to the thyroid cartilage, a distinct attachment); the thyrohyoid membrane (connects the hyoid bone to the thyroid cartilage, lateral to this ligament) [formal: ligamentum hyoepiglotticum | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
